newsitem.title: INDIA: India moves to attract more foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: India moves to attract more foreign investment.

text.p: India eased a restriction on foreign investment on Friday in an effort to accelerate development of capital-starved infrastructure projects that are essential to economic growth.

The move would allow foreign firms, currently limited to a 49 percent direct stake in expensive infrastructure services such as telecommunications, to take an additional indirect stake of up to 25 percent.
Although India began opening its doors to foreign investment in 1991, flows of foreign funds into key areas such as telecommunications, ports, roads and power have fallen far short of expectations.
Earlier this week, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda lamented the fact that India has lagged far behind China in attracting foreign investment.
In 1994, China pulled in $33.8 billion of foreign direct investment compared to India's $620 million, according to the World Bank.
Analysts say the relatively slow development of infrastructure, especially power, has created bottlenecks which are beginning to strangle economic growth.
"These companies are not able to raise adequate funds in the domestic market," the government said in a statement. "Therefore, many projects are yet to take off."

The government said in a statement that the Cabinet Committee on Foreign Investment took "some important decisions" at a meeting on Thursday aimed at attracting more funds into the sluggish infrastructure sector.
Currently foreign firms can take no more than a 49 percent stake in joint ventures in the infrastructure sector.

The Indian cabinet committee exempted "investing", or shell, companies which take a stake in a joint infrastructure venture from a cap on foreign investment, even if an overseas firm owns a share of the shell firm.
The decision had the effect of allowing foreign firms to pump more money into Indian projects because any investment channelled through the shell companies would be considered as a domestic stake.
Under the new guidelines, foreign firms could effectively take up to a 74 percent stake in the joint venture, with 49 percent as a direct stake and 25 percent indirect.
But the Indian partner would continue to control the joint venture.
"This arrangement will also enable the domestic companies which have the inherent strength of raising finance to start up operations of their business," it said.
